transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-27
Time: 10:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jenna Li (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood CSM), Lena Torres (NimbleHealth Head of ML), Rajesh Kumar (Infra), Maya O'Connor (PM)

Summary: weekly POC caching sync — review of KV/prefix cache hit rates, prompt reuse strategy, recent tuning changes and next steps.

[00:00] Samir Patel: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, uh quick agenda — hit rates, tuning notes, next steps.
[00:18] Lena Torres: yeah thanks, we saw the dashboard, yep excited to dig in.
[00:22] Jenna Li: quick note — i pushed the recent KV cache config last night, TTLs lowered for ephemeral prompts and we enabled prefix caching for the chat endpoints.
[00:35] Rajesh Kumar: i saw that, dashboard shows KV hit rate jumped but transcription says K-V cash, so, uh.
[00:42] Jenna Li: yeah the KV cache — we measured an overall hit rate of about 62% this morning, up from ~45% last week after aggressive normalization. prefix cache hits are around 38%.
[00:55] Maya O'Connor: is that aggregate across all intents? some of our high-variance prompts still show low reuse.
[01:06] Jenna Li: correct, the long-tail of prompts with dynamic placeholders drags overall. for the top 10 intents we get ~78% KV hit and prefix hit near 55%.
[01:24] Samir Patel: that maps to observed latency improvements — p50 down ~18% and p95 down ~12% for the top workloads. numbers vary for low-frequency flows.
[01:38] Lena Torres: can you explain what changed in normalization? our engineers reported they removed punctuation and canonicalized dates but we want the exact approach.
[01:50] Jenna Li: sure — pipeline did three things: 1) template extraction (convert dynamic fields to placeholders), 2) whitespace and punctuation normalization, 3) lowercase and limited token truncation to consistent prefix length. also we added conversation-id based keys so kv entries are widespread only when appropriate.
[02:12] Rajesh Kumar: conversation-id keys — does that fragment cache more? we worry about cardinality.
[02:20] Jenna Li: good question — we used a hybrid key: model+intent+normalized_prefix, and conversation-id only for session-scoped entries (TTL 5m). global KV keys exclude conversation id. this avoids high cardinality.
[02:36] Maya O'Connor: ok that helps. what about prompt reuse — we have many micro-variations like "please summarize in bullet points" vs "give bullets" — how do we unify?
[02:46] Jenna Li: the recommendation is to create canonical templates in the app layer — e.g., a single summary template with variables. we can also put a small canonicalizer in the client library to rewrite common paraphrases to the canonical template before sending to the server, which increases prefix cache match.
[03:02] Lena Torres: would Redwood provide a helper lib for canonicalization?
[03:05] Samir Patel: yes we can share a tiny JS/Python snippet as a starting point — not a full NLP paraphrase system, but rule-based rewrites for high-frequency variants.
[03:16] Rajesh Kumar: on infra — TTLs for prefix vs KV, what's recommended? our current TTL was 24h for kv, which may be too long for dynamic user data.
[03:26] Jenna Li: recommended default: KV entries derived from deterministic inputs (user profile merges) — TTL 24h, but ephemeral generation keys — TTL 5-30 minutes depending on freshness, prefix cache (shared prompts) TTL 12h for templates. We tuned one of your longer TTLs down which unlocked more hit rate because it avoided cache pollution.
[03:48] Maya O'Connor: you mentioned cache pollution — can you expand?
[03:50] Jenna Li: sure — when a one-off prompt with long context writes a kv key and it sticks around with a long TTL, it consumes slots and reduces hit rates for common templates. evictions happen LRU-style on our side, but TTL tuning plus canonicalization reduces pollution.
[04:08] Samir Patel: quick interjection — we also recommend a small admission policy: don't cache responses that are under a certain randomness/temperature threshold or contain user-specific confidential bits.
[04:20] Lena Torres: makes sense for PHI, especially for us in health domain. any encryption/KKMS notes?
[04:25] Samir Patel: for Private/Dedicated deployments you'd use your KMS; for hosted we support envelope encryption and redact PHI before caching. we can share SOC2 docs and the security sheet.
[04:38] Rajesh Kumar: please share the security sheet in the shared drive.
[04:42] Samir Patel: will do.
[04:45] Jenna Li: returning to metrics — we ran a 6h synthetic run yesterday with mixed workload: result summary is attached in the bench spreadsheet (link pasted in chat). Highlights: overall KV hit 62%, prefix hit 38%, top-10 intents prefix hit 55%, average token cost down 14% for top flows. latency p50 improvement 18% for top flows.
[05:12] Lena Torres: that 62% — is that measured after dedup/normalization?
[05:16] Jenna Li: yes after normalization and the updated key scheme. raw (no normalization) would have been ~41%.
[05:22] Maya O'Connor: can we run a 24h run on real-ish traffic? that would help convince compliance and infra.
[05:28] Samir Patel: agree — Jenna can run a 24h KV cache stress run using masked production traces and post the spreadsheet.
[05:33] Jenna Li: i'll start that tonight, will anonymize and mask PII.
[05:38] Rajesh Kumar: note: our infra team wants to test eviction behavior under sustained writes — we'll provide a short workload pattern file.
[05:44] Samir Patel: good, send that to me and jenna.
[05:46] Lena Torres: question on metrics instrumentation — are we sending token-level cost and per-key hit metrics to our console?
[05:54] Jenna Li: yes, Redwood Console shows per-route token cost, KV hit/miss counts and TTL histograms. we'll give you dashboard access if you want to pin it.
[06:04] Maya O'Connor: i saw an occasional miss where the system returned a near duplicate instead of a cached exact response — is that fallback logic?
[06:11] Jenna Li: yes if a cached response is from a different model variant we may apply similarity fallback, or supply candidate rerank. that was by design to avoid big regressions when a model variant was unavailable. it'll be flagged in the logs as a fallback event.
[06:30] Rajesh Kumar: any guidance for model variant routing vs cache? we have two variants: fast-quantized and higher-quality.
[06:36] Samir Patel: route by policy — prefer fast quantized for low-cost queries but allow quality variant for gold-intents. caching keys should include model variant label when semantic differences are expected. that reduces incorrect cache reuse across variants.
[06:50] Lena Torres: timeline — what's next week look like? are we on track for pilot benchmark review?
[06:57] Samir Patel: yes if we get the 24h run and your prompt flows this week, we can present a consolidated pilot metrics deck next Tuesday.
[07:06] Maya O'Connor: confirmed we'll send prompt flows by Friday.
[07:10] Jenna Li: quick note: we've added a low-priority ticket to normalize date formats as you had asked — should reduce long-tail variants.
[07:18] Carlos Mendes: thanks team — from CSM side i'll capture the follow ups.
[07:22] Samir Patel: ok recap — jenna runs 24h stress run, samir shares config and README, nimble sends canonical prompt flows, redwood shares security docs and dashboard access.
[07:35] Lena Torres: thanks all, useful sync.
[07:40] Samir Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.

References/links mentioned in chat: bench spreadsheet (https://redwood.app/bench/nimblehealth-caching-2026-10), security sheet (shared drive link), config gist (will be shared by Samir).

Meeting end.
